review.review_summary: 9 claims checked against the evidence; 4 flagged (1 unsupported, 2 overstated).
gaps: The report does not show whether Support's attrition rate is higher than other departments' attrition rates over the 12-month period, which would be needed to support the claim that Support loses the most people.
No evidence covers whether the 62 Support exits in Jun 2026 were voluntary or involuntary, which is critical to understanding whether pay is a driver or whether the event was a planned reduction.
The report does not analyze attrition by job level, worker type, or tenure, which could reveal whether the attrition spike reflects a specific cohort or a broad workforce issue.
next_investigations: Compare attrition rate (separations ÷ average headcount) by department over the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026 to determine which department actually loses the most people as a proportion of its workforce.
Analyze the 62 Support exits in Jun 2026 by termination category to determine whether they were voluntary or involuntary and whether they reflect a planned reduction or unplanned attrition.
Segment attrition by annual salary quartile within Support to test whether lower-paid employees in that department have higher attrition than higher-paid employees.
methodology_concerns: Five rows have an ended employment status but no termination date, and 5 records are dated after 31 Oct 2026 (not yet counted). These 10 data gaps affect the completeness of the 29.6% attrition rate and the Jun 2026 count of 79 separations.

The evidence notes that 41 of 1,729 people have more than one row in the dataset. The analysis counts rows (1,770), not unique people (1,729), which could affect department-level and monthly separation counts if rehires or transfers are not clearly identified.

claims.text: Low pay is driving attrition: Support, the lowest-paid department, loses the most people, so raising Support salaries would cut its attrition.
The surge in total attrition masks a slight fall in voluntary attrition, and a single month — Jun 2026 — accounts for a disproportionate share of exits, concentrated in one department.

Total attrition reached 29.6% in the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, up from 22.8% a year earlier (+6.8 points), yet voluntary attrition moved in the opposite direction, falling from 16.9% to 15.9% over the same comparison — meaning the rise is largely involuntary.
Attrition so far in 2026 is 26.2%, an annual attrition rate of 31.4% if the pace holds, the highest in four years.
Only 2 women in Legal left this year, both from the same team.
Ten Support employees are flight risks and should be put on retention plans now.

Investigate the Jun 2026 Support department event: determine whether the 62 exits were a planned reduction or unplanned, and document the business rationale. Explains the majority of the attrition spike and informs whether further headcount loss is expected.

Monitor involuntary attrition separately from voluntary attrition in monthly reporting, given they moved in opposite directions over the past year. Prevents the total attrition figure from masking different underlying workforce dynamics.

Review the 5 rows with an ended status but no termination date and the 5 records dated after 31 Oct 2026 to ensure separation counts and attrition figures are complete. Small data gaps could affect the accuracy of the reported 29.6% attrition rate.

Read as HR data (headcount, FTE, separations, attrition rate, voluntary attrition, hires, average salary (current staff)). Headcount is the people in force at the latest date (contractors and agency workers out, interns and part-timers in); separations and hires are events (a rehire's exits count separately); attrition is separations ÷ the average of the month-end headcounts over the 12 months to that date. Pay and protected attributes (gender, ethnicity) are never shown for groups of fewer than 11 people.
Gender is shown as a description only: hiring, firing or pay decisions on it are discrimination, so no recommendation is made on it; groups of fewer than 11 people are not shown.
Ethnicity is special-category data (GDPR Art. 9): shown as a description only, never a recommendation about people, and never for groups of fewer than 11.
Performance ratings describe groups here; they are never used to rank or predict individuals.

Pay is annual base salary as recorded: part-time salaries are not full-time equivalents, so groups with more part-timers (often women) show lower pay than on a full-time-equivalent basis, which the unadjusted pay gap uses; pay is never shown for a group of fewer than 11 people.

gaps: The analysis does not examine attrition by department, which is needed to understand whether the overall 6.7-point improvement is evenly distributed or concentrated in specific areas.
No breakdown of hires and separations by cohort or tenure is shown, so the claim that new joiners drove attrition cannot be validated or explored.
The analysis does not compare salary levels between employees who separated and those who remained, which could help explain attrition drivers.
next_investigations: Segment attrition rate by department for both 12-month periods (to Oct 2025 and to Oct 2026) to determine whether the 6.7-point improvement is evenly distributed or concentrated in one or two departments.
Analyze separations by tenure cohort (time between hire date and termination date) to test whether new joiners have higher separation rates than tenured employees.
Compare average base salary between employees who separated in the past 12 months and those still in force as of 31 October 2026, segmented by department.

claims.text: A workforce of 353 employees is stabilising: the 12-month attrition rate fell to 14.3% by October 2026, down from 20.9% a year earlier.
The dataset covers 24 months of monthly HR snapshots (Nov 2024 – Oct 2026) across 8,220 employees, tracking headcount, pay, hires, and separations.
Hiring 70 people in 12 months is what pushed attrition up to 14.3%: the new joiners left first.
Attrition has improved materially: the 12-month rate to October 2026 is 14.3%, compared with 20.9% for the 12 months to October 2025, a drop of 6.7 points.
The workforce stands at 353 employees (338.40 FTE) as of 31 October 2026, with hires (70) outpacing separations (49) over the past 12 months, indicating net headcount growth.
Average base salary across all records ranges from $34,400.00 to $170,800.00, with a median of $82,700.00 and a mean of $84,622.10; salary outliers at the high end have been flagged but retained.
Average base salary by department ranges from $83,436.67 in Finance to $87,825.00 in Marketing, with Engineering, Operations, and Sales sitting close together in between.

Investigate what changed between the two 12-month periods to understand what is associated with the attrition improvement, and assess whether the conditions driving it are sustainable. Protects the gains already made and informs retention strategy going forward.

Review the high-end base salary outliers flagged in the data to confirm they are correct records before using pay figures in any compensation benchmarking. Prevents skewed averages from distorting pay decisions.
Segment attrition by department to determine whether the overall improvement is evenly distributed or concentrated in one area. Identifies departments that may still carry elevated turnover risk.
